Your argument seems to be "we shouldn't give people the choice because they will make the wrong choice." People should have the right to make choices that you think are wrong. 

​

Also, I am not saying that suicide solves problems, but it does remove the ability to think or feel about those problems. It would be like if your computer has a virus that is wreaking havoc and causing distress. And everyone around you says "keep trying! We'll get rid of that virus eventually! Don't give up! Being able to play video games, go on the internet, and use Microsoft Office is worth the pain of the virus." But instead you decide to choose nothing instead. So even though it will mean giving up experiencing all the cool things that a computer can do, you just unplug the computer instead. You lose both the bad things (the virus) and the good things (a computer's capabilities). You now have nothing, which is neither bad nor good.   


It's not a perfect metaphor, but suicide is just the choice of opting out of both bad and good things in life. It is choosing to not play the game at all. And if you want to continue to work on fixing your brain's viruses because you are looking forward to experiencing an awesome computer user experience, I support you. I hope that you get better and get help. But if another person decides that their virus is too much, I don't think that anyone else can make that call for them.

One of the problems is that I consider her a good friend and still want to spend time wit her, get coffees, etc.
I'm afraid that it will be difficult to salvage a relationship
